name: CPU architecture via float behavior
plain: Telling ARM from x86 by how Float32 values behave in JavaScript.
meaning: FingerprintJS writes a Float32Array and reads bytes to detect endianness-like behavior. Chromium reduced UA hides CPU, but such probes can infer the architecture class anyway.

access.persistence: read fresh on every page load; nothing stored
access.iframe: Readable from cross-origin iframes too (same values)

limits.headline: Can run number tests to tell whether your chip is ARM or x86
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads
can: Store numbers in memory and check how they behave
Guess your chip family, such as ARM or x86
Work even when Chrome hides the chip in its browser label
cannot: See your files or what you typed
Know who you are by itself

story.what_it_is: A script tells ARM chips from Intel style chips by how tiny decimal numbers behave in JavaScript.
story.for_you: You never see it. Your chip does a math trick in a hidden way and the answer shows whether it is an Apple or phone style chip or a PC style chip.
story.for_makers: It lets fraud tools check that the chip matches the claimed device, such as a phone that claims to be a Mac. Trackers add it to a device ID. Sites rarely need it for features.

use_cases.example: A fraud tool sees a device claim to be an Intel laptop but behave like a phone chip, and flags an emulator.
A tracker uses the chip type as one more small piece of a device ID.
A visitor tool splits users by chip family to learn how many use Apple silicon or ARM Windows.
A game studio gathers chip types to decide which builds of a web game need testing.
A developer finds why a number result looks different on one chip and fixes the bug.
A bank compares chip type with the device model on file to spot a copied profile.
A retailer checks that a device really is the phone it claims to be, to catch bots.
